description_short: Trump: 1pm: Pipe bombs, a riot, and the Senate Sergeant at Arms refuses to call the National Guard
description_medium: At 1 p.m. on January 6, 2021, Capitol Police Chief Steven Sund asked House Sergeant at Arms Paul Irving to authorize National Guard support, then made the same request to Senate Sergeant at Arms Michael Stenger at 1:05 p.m. The request came as rioters breached the Capitol during Congress’s electoral vote count.
description_long:
On January 6, 2021, as rioters attacked the U.S. Capitol and Congress met to count electoral votes, Capitol Police Chief Steven Sund sought National Guard assistance. The New York Times timeline places the request at Sund asked House Sergeant at Arms Paul Irving to declare an emergency and call in the Guard. At 1:05 p.m., he made the same request to Senate Sergeant at Arms Michael Stenger.

The timing matters because the request came during a fast-moving breach, when congressional offices and lawmakers were under threat. The episode later became central to investigations of security preparations and the chain of command at the Capitol. The title characterizes Stenger as refusing the request, but the cited timeline establishes when Sund made it without detailing Stenger’s response. The precise decision process and reasons for delay require fuller documentation. The event illustrates how responsibility for emergency assistance was divided among Capitol security officials during the attack.

title: Trump Reinstates Schedule F — Converts Career Civil Servants to At-Will Political Employees
description_short: Trump Reinstates Schedule F — Converts Career Civil Servants to At-Will Political Employees
description_medium: On January 20, 2025, Trump signed an order reviving Schedule F, a federal employment category intended to make certain policy-related career positions easier to reclassify and remove. The order reversed a Biden administration rule and set up expected legal challenges over civil-service protections and presidential control of the federal workforce.
description_long:
On January 20, 2025, Trump signed an executive order reviving Schedule F, a category he had created shortly before the 2020 election. The order sought to replace a Biden-era rule and give the administration more control over federal employees in policy-related positions. Under the framework, agencies could reclassify some career jobs, reducing the procedural protections that ordinarily apply to civil servants.

The administration presented the change as a way to improve accountability and performance. Critics warned that moving career positions into a more politically controlled category could make it easier to remove experienced officials and replace them with political appointees. That risk is distinct from the order’s stated goal: the practical effects depend on how agencies classify positions and how courts interpret the protections that remain. The order was expected to face legal challenges. Its significance lies in the balance it seeks to change between presidential direction and an independent professional civil service. The order’s effects depend on how agencies classify positions and how courts resolve challenges to its implementation. Accounts describe injunctions in multiple jurisdictions, but their scope and status remain unclear.

title: Wilbur Ross Commerce Secretary Conflicts — Maintained Stake in Companies He Regulated
description_short: Wilbur Ross Commerce Secretary Conflicts — Maintained Stake in Companies He Regulated
description_medium: As Commerce secretary, Wilbur Ross retained an investment in Diamond S Shipping, a tanker company with business involving ports in countries subject to U.S. sanctions. The Center for Public Integrity reported that the holding raised conflict-of-interest questions as Ross took a prominent role in Trump’s trade policy; Ross said he would be a passive investor and did not consider it a conflict.
description_long:
Wilbur Ross became Commerce secretary while retaining an investment in Diamond S Shipping, a tanker company whose business included routes and ports connected to countries subject to U.S. sanctions. The Center for Public Integrity reported that Ross planned to keep the stake while stepping down from company positions and serving as a passive investor. The company disclosed that it could call at ports in sanctioned countries, including Iran, Cuba, Sudan, and Syria.

The holding raised questions about whether Ross’s private financial interests could intersect with his work shaping trade policy. Ethics lawyers cited in the reporting differed on whether the investment created a conflict, and Ross said he did not believe it did. The article describes a potential conflict and a disclosure issue; it does not establish that Ross used his office to benefit the company. The distinction matters because an investment can create an appearance or management problem without proof of a specific official act. The episode illustrates the scrutiny applied to financial disclosures and divestment commitments for senior officials.

title: Musk's DOGE Given Access to $6 Trillion Treasury Payment System
description_short: Musk's DOGE Given Access to $6 Trillion Treasury Payment System
description_medium: In early February 2025, Treasury gave a DOGE-affiliated technology executive read-only access to federal payment systems that disburse more than $6 trillion annually. The systems handle payments including Social Security, Medicare, and federal salaries. Treasury said the access was read-only; critics raised privacy and security concerns, and career official David Lebryk resigned.
description_long:
In early February 2025, Treasury granted a DOGE-affiliated technology executive read-only access to federal payment systems. Those systems process more than $6 trillion in annual disbursements, including Social Security, Medicare, and federal payroll. Treasury told lawmakers the access was read-only. The decision prompted concern because the systems contain sensitive financial and personal information and are essential to routine government payments.

The access dispute also coincided with the resignation of David Lebryk, a senior career Treasury official. Democrats and security experts warned that access to sensitive system data could create privacy and cybersecurity risks, while the administration described the access as limited. Read-only access does not itself authorize changing or stopping payments; the concerns centered on the scope of information available and the safeguards around it. The episode became part of wider legal and congressional scrutiny of DOGE’s access to government data. The $6 trillion figure refers to annual payment throughput, not an account balance or new spending authority. Treasury’s “read-only” characterization was disputed by critics concerned about the scope of access and safeguards.

title: Trump Withdraws from Trans-Pacific Partnership — Gift to China
subcategory: Trade Policy and U.S. Withdrawal from TPP
description_short: Trump Withdraws from Trans-Pacific Partnership — Gift to China
description_medium: On January 23, 2017, Trump directed the United States to withdraw as a signatory to the Trans-Pacific Partnership and end its participation in negotiations. His memorandum called for bilateral trade talks instead. The decision fulfilled a campaign pledge but removed the United States from a regional trade framework negotiated with 11 other Pacific Rim countries.
description_long:
Trump signed a memorandum on January 23, 2017 directing the United States to withdraw as a signatory to the Trans-Pacific Partnership and leave its negotiations. The order also instructed the U.S. trade representative to notify the other parties and pursue bilateral agreements. It fulfilled a campaign promise to reject a large multilateral trade pact and return to country-by-country negotiations.

The TPP involved 12 Pacific Rim countries and had been negotiated under the Obama administration. Supporters argued that its common rules and market access would strengthen U.S. economic engagement in Asia; critics objected to its terms and effects on workers. The U.S. withdrawal ended American participation in that agreement, while the remaining countries later moved forward without the United States. Analysts warned that withdrawal could reduce U.S. influence over regional trade rules and leave space for China to expand its role. Those are strategic assessments, not consequences established by the memorandum itself. The order records a significant shift in trade policy toward bilateral negotiations and away from the regional framework.

title: Trump: ‘So shameful’: backlash as US national monuments conform to Trump’s rewrite of history
description_short: Trump: ‘So shameful’: backlash as US national monuments conform to Trump’s rewrite of history
description_medium: ‘So shameful’: backlash as US national monuments conform to Trump’s rewrite of history. description_long:
The Guardian reported that federal monuments and historic sites changed displays about racism and Indigenous history under Trump’s effort to revise what he called ‘woke’ presentations. At Philadelphia’s President’s House, panels describing slavery were removed, leaving blank spaces where the exhibit had stood. The changes drew criticism from historians and visitors, including people who said the displays explained the lives of enslaved people at the site.

The administration’s approach treated interpretation of national history as a policy issue, directing agencies to review exhibits and remove material viewed as divisive or inconsistent with the president’s priorities. Critics argued that removing references to slavery, racism, and Indigenous dispossession erased documented history from public spaces. These responses describe the dispute over the changes; they do not establish that every monument was altered in the same way. The episode shows how executive priorities can shape the content visitors encounter at federally managed sites. The consequences include a public debate over who determines how national history is presented and what historical evidence is made visible.
